title: Distillery Visitor Centres and Tours | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan a distillery visitor centre and tours in India: safe routes, tastings within the rules, staffing and what visitors want.
teaser: A good tour turns a visitor into a lifelong customer. A badly planned one walks them past a hot still into a hazardous area.
standfirst: Visitors want to see where whisky is made, smell the mash and taste at the end. A distillery tour can earn steady money and build a brand. It also brings strangers into a plant full of flammable spirit, so it needs careful planning from the first drawing.
sections:
Whisky drinkers like to visit distilleries. A tour gives them a story to tell and a bottle to take home. For a craft distillery, that story is worth more than an advertisement, especially in India, where direct advertising of alcohol is not allowed. A visitor who has seen your stills is likely to look for your whisky on a menu.

Tours also bring direct revenue: ticket income, merchandise and, where the rules allow, bottle sales and tastings. For a distillery waiting years for its first whisky, that steady income helps.

A distillery handles ethanol vapour, steam, hot surfaces and heavy moving equipment. Areas around stills, spirit receivers and filling stations are usually classified as hazardous areas, where vapour may be present and ignition sources must be controlled. Our guide to hazardous area zoning in a distillery explains the classification.

Visitors should never walk through those zones. The common solution is a raised gallery or a glass wall that gives a clear view of the stills without entering the area. Plan this from the start. Adding a visitor route to an existing plant is expensive and often awkward.

  • No phones or cameras with flash in classified areas unless they are approved for it.
  • Clear signage, handrails and non-slip floors.
  • Guides trained in emergency evacuation.
  • A headcount at the start and end of every tour.

Most visitors want the same few things: the raw grain, the smell of the mash tun, washbacks bubbling, copper stills and casks in a warehouse. A short, well told sequence beats a long technical lecture.

A simple route might go grain, mash, fermentation, stills, warehouse, tasting. At each stop, one clear fact works better than five. For example: "This wash is around 8% ABV, about as strong as a strong beer. The stills will take it to around 70%." Visitors remember numbers like that.

Warehouses deserve care. They are full of spirit. The vapour can build up in still air. Keep visitors to a viewing area or a sample warehouse with good ventilation and no ignition sources.

Tasting rules in India depend on the state. Some states allow sampling at a distillery under a specific licence. Others restrict it heavily or not at all. Rules on selling bottles at the distillery also vary. Check the current excise rules before you promise a tasting on your website.

Where tastings are allowed, keep them responsible: small measures of around 15 ml, water on every table, food available and no pressure to finish. Ask who is driving and offer them a sample to take home sealed, or a non-alcoholic alternative. Check ages at the door. Anyone under the state's legal drinking age should not be served.

Guides make or break a tour. They need to know the process well enough to answer any question honestly, from "why copper?" to "how long does it age?" Train them on the production side, not just a script. A guide who can explain why the wash is not boiled before fermentation earns respect from serious visitors.

Think about pace and group size. A group of 10 to 15 people can hear the guide and see the stills. A group of 40 cannot. Book tours in time slots so groups do not bunch up at the stills.

A visitor centre only works if people can reach it. A distillery within a short drive of a city or on a tourist route will see far more visitors than one in a remote valley. If you are still choosing a site, our guide to choosing a site for a distillery in India covers the trade-offs.

Parking, toilets, shade and drinking water matter more than people expect, especially in Indian summer heat.

A visitor centre shop can sell much more than whisky. Glassware, books, clothing, local food and gin where it is permitted all add income without any of the licensing questions that come with selling spirit. Where state rules allow bottle sales at the distillery, a distillery-only bottling gives visitors a reason to buy on the spot.

Events bring repeat visitors. A cask filling day, a festival of the distillery's own spirit or a talk on maturation can fill the calendar in quieter months. Keep each one within the rules on serving alcohol and with the same responsible approach as the tour: small measures, water, food and no pressure.

Track numbers from the start: visitors per month, spend per visitor and how many come back. Those figures tell you whether the visitor centre is paying its way.

Draw your distillery's floor plan and trace a visitor route on it in a different colour. Mark every hazardous area. Where the route crosses one, redesign it. Then write one sentence a guide would say at each stop. If you struggle to write those sentences clearly, train yourself and your guides on the process before the first visitor arrives.
faqs: Can visitors taste whisky at an Indian distillery?
It depends on the state. Some allow sampling under a specific licence, others do not. Check the current excise rules before offering tastings.
How do distilleries keep visitors safe?
By keeping visitor routes out of hazardous areas, often with viewing galleries or glass walls, plus signage, trained guides and evacuation plans.
How large should a distillery tour group be?
Around 10 to 15 people lets everyone hear the guide and see the equipment clearly.
